How much to charge for a French drain

The number a homeowner wants is a published “$25 a foot installed” special, or a “$40 a linear foot” coupon. That number is not a takeoff. A 40-foot shallow 4-inch daylight trench in dirt is not the same job as an 80-foot deep 6-inch run in clay that has to hit a drywell, two catch basins, three downspout ties, and a driveway crossing. The trip is the same. The hours are not.

Open the free bid calculator

Count the trench and the extras, not just “a French drain”

Basement-waterproofing calculators price interior perimeter drain, window wells, and a sump pit. Gutter-install calculators price K-style, miters, and fascia. An exterior yard drain is a different job: the trench, the pipe, the outlet, and the extras that are not in the coupon. Quoting all of that from a published per-foot special is how the first rock ledge and the first saw-cut eat the field margin.

A job with the same trip can cost much more

Each extra foot of depth is time and gravel that never appears on the coupon. Clay, a drywell, catch basins, downspout ties, and a driveway crossing are billed as their own hours. On the sample rates an 80-foot deep 6-inch clay drywell run with two basins, three downspouts, a 15-foot driveway crossing, lawn restore, and tear-out of spoils prices about $8,824.85 (45.3 crew-hours, $110.31 per foot). The same shop’s 40-foot shallow daylight trench prices about $1,862.64 (9.3 hours, walk-away $1,303.85, $46.57 per foot). Matching the brochure job’s $25/ft special ($1,000 on 40 feet, $2,000 on 80 feet) on the clay drywell yard is how that job becomes a loss — the walk-away on the heavy job is already $6,177.40, and the $2,000 special loses about $4,177 there. The $1,000 special loses $303.85 even on the brochure trench.

A storm tie-in and extra solid pipe are not automatically a markup on daylight

A 50-foot standard 4-inch storm tap with one basin and 30 feet of solid pipe to the outlet is not the 40-foot brochure trench plus 15%. On the sample rates that storm job prices about $3,829.47 (18.8 crew-hours). A daylight outlet drops drywell hours; depth and clay do not disappear with the daylight. Treating either as a blended add-on is how the special that looked fine turns into a loss after the first rock ledge.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $42/h operator loaded at 30% payroll burden is $54.60. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. Replace every rate with your invoices before you send either number.

What this is not

This is not a drainage design, a building-code determination, a permit, an engineering stamp, or a recommended market price. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. The run, the depth, pipe, soil, outlet, and basins are yours to confirm. It does not price an interior basement waterproofing job or a gutter install.

Price your French drain

Common questions

How much to charge for a French drain?

Charge from the trip, the trench (depth times soil), pipe size, the outlet (daylight, drywell, or storm tie-in), catch basins, downspout ties, driveway crossings, extra solid pipe, lawn restore, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default 40-foot shallow 4-inch daylight trench in dirt, at the sample rates in this calculator, prices around $1,863 — about 9.3 crew-hours, $46.57 per foot.

Why is a $25-a-foot French drain special dangerous?

Homeowners count linear feet. Depth, clay, a drywell, basins, and a driveway do not scale with that number. Matching a cheaper special written for a 40-foot daylight trench is how an 80-foot clay drywell job becomes a two-day loss. On the sample rates the $25/ft special already loses about $304 on the brochure trench (walk-away $1,304) and loses about $4,177 on the clay drywell yard whose walk-away is already $6,177.

How much to charge for a deep French drain with a drywell?

An 80-foot deep 6-inch run in clay with a drywell, two catch basins, three downspout ties, and a 15-foot driveway crossing is not a 40-foot shallow special. On the sample rates that job prices around $8,825 (45.3 crew-hours, $110.31 per foot), while a 40-foot shallow daylight trench prices around $1,863 (9.3 hours).

      Common questions

      Why can a competitor advertise “$25 a foot” for a French drain?

      Because a per-foot price is written around the easiest possible trench, and that trench is the first preset here: 40 feet, shallow, 4-inch perforated, daylighted to grade, in dirt, with the lawn put back. Everything that makes a wet-basement job hard — depth, clay or rock, a drywell or a storm tie-in, catch basins, downspout ties, going under a driveway — is not in that number. Price the actual yard beside the special and the difference becomes line items you can point at.

      How much does digging deeper really cost?

      It moves labor and gravel together, which is why depth is the biggest lever on this page. A shallow 18-inch trench starts at 0.12 hours and $4.50 of gravel per foot. Standard 24–30 inch goes to 0.16 hours and $6.40. A deep 36–48 inch trench is 0.22 hours and $9.20 — nearly double the shallow number on both sides at once. Depth is decided by where the water is, not by the bid, so it is worth settling before you quote a rate.

      Why does soil type multiply the price instead of adding to it?

      Because it scales with every foot you dig. The soil factor multiplies the trench hours only — not the outlet, not the extras — at 1× in dirt or loam, 1.45× in clay, and 2.1× in rock or hardpan. It moves the spoils dump too: $85, $185, and $320 respectively, because rock and clay come out heavier and cost more to take away. A 60-foot run in rock is not a 60-foot run with a surcharge; it is more than twice the digging.

      What’s the difference between daylighting, a drywell, and a storm tie-in?

      Where the water is allowed to go, and it is the second-largest swing here. Daylighting to grade is 1.5 hours and no kit — free, if the grade cooperates. A drywell or pop-up emitter is 3.8 hours and a $380 kit because it is a second excavation. A storm or catch-basin tie-in is 4.2 hours and a $265 kit, and is usually the one that needs a permit and an inspection your jurisdiction sets, so the permit fee is its own field and starts at zero rather than being guessed for you.

      Why are catch basins, downspout ties, and driveway crossings priced one at a time?

      Because a drain that solves the problem is rarely just the trench. Each catch basin is 1.2 hours plus a $165 kit; each downspout tie is 0.6 hours plus a $45 kit; going under a driveway is 0.35 hours per foot, the most expensive foot on the job. Solid (non-perforated) pipe carrying water past where you do not want it collecting runs 0.08 hours and $2.40 a foot. Tick only what the yard actually needs and the price follows the scope instead of a package.

      Is my data uploaded anywhere?

      No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. Your bid is saved in this browser’s local storage so it is still here next visit, and a bid link you copy carries those same numbers in the page’s address rather than sending anything to a server. The optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your footage, wages, or prices.

      What’s the difference between the bid price and the walk-away price?

      The bid price already carries your target margin on top of labor, materials, fees, and overhead. The walk-away price is the total cost underneath it — crew hours, pipe, gravel, fabric, the outlet kit, basins and ties, spoils disposal, lawn restore, permit, travel and equipment — the point below which the dig stops being profitable at all. Typing a number into “Price you’re considering” shows you the margin, or the loss, before you send it.

vs-a-flat-price-per-foot.html.text:
← French Drain Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat price per foot

French-drain contractors are shopped by a flat price per foot. That rate cannot see the job — depth, pipe size, soil, the outlet, catch basins, and a driveway crossing do not scale with linear footage, and an 80-foot run can take five times the labor of a 40-foot run.

What a flat price per foot is

A price per foot is the fastest number to quote over the phone: pace off the run, multiply by a rate, read back a total. It is also the unit homeowners already compare between competing bids.

The rate behind it was learned from a specific job — a given depth, soil, and outlet — and then reused for the next linear footage that calls in, whether or not that next job shares any of those.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter linear feet, trench depth, pipe size, soil, the outlet (daylight, drywell, or storm tie-in), catch basins, downspout ties, a driveway crossing, and extra solid pipe to the outlet, plus your own wage, payroll burden, material rates, travel, overhead, and target margin. It prices the trench, the outlet, and every extra as their own hours and cost lines — for this job, not a rate carried over from the last one.

What a flat per-foot rate doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same rate for an 18-inch trench in loam and a 36-to-48-inch trench in clay or rock, even though depth and soil are most of the labor. Prices trench hours from depth and a soil hour factor, so a deep clay run costs more without anyone eyeballing a surcharge.
Has no line for the outlet — daylighting to grade, a drywell pit, and a permitted storm tie-in get the same rate. Prices outlet hours and kit cost separately by outlet type.
Has no line for catch basins, downspout ties, extra solid pipe, or a driveway crossing at all. Prices each of those as its own hours and material, on top of linear footage.
Bills pipe size inside the same blended per-foot number, if at all. Prices a 6-inch pipe's extra material cost and hour premium separately from a 4-inch run.
Gives the crew a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the price per foot and the walk-away price alongside the total, so a shopped rate can be scored against real cost before you match it.

Same trade, two different jobs

Using this calculator's own shipped cost inputs — $42 hourly wage, 30% burden, $95 travel and equipment, 15% overhead, 30% target margin:

A 40-foot shallow daylight trench in dirt, with a lawn restore, takes 9.3 crew-hours and prices at $1,862.64 for the job — $46.57 per foot.

An 80-foot deep drywell run in clay — twice the footage — with two catch basins, three downspout ties, and a 15-foot driveway crossing takes 45.3 crew-hours, costs $6,177.40 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator prices it at $8,824.85 — $110.31 per foot. Quoting the deep job at the shallow job's learned rate of $46.57 per foot gives $3,725.28 for eighty feet, which is $2,452.12 below the deep job's own break-even cost — before counting the $5,099.58 it falls short of this calculator's own price at a 30% target margin. Twice the footage, roughly five times the labor, and a rate learned on the shallow job loses money the moment the trencher hits clay.

Common questions

Why does a flat price per foot get a French-drain bid wrong?

Because linear footage only measures how long the trench is, not what it takes to dig and finish it. A 40-foot shallow daylight trench in dirt takes about 9.3 crew-hours. An 80-foot deep drywell run in clay with two catch basins, three downspout ties, and a 15-foot driveway crossing takes about 45.3 crew-hours -- twice the footage, roughly five times the labor, because depth, soil, the outlet, and the extras do not scale with linear feet.

What does a flat per-foot rate usually miss entirely?

Trench depth, pipe size, soil type, the outlet, catch basins, downspout ties, and a driveway crossing. A flat rate has no line for the difference between an 18-inch trench in loam and a 36-to-48-inch trench in clay or rock, no line for daylighting to grade versus a drywell pit or a permitted storm tie-in, and no line for catch basins, downspout ties, extra solid pipe, or cutting and patching a driveway at all.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

Using this calculator's own shipped cost inputs: a 40-foot shallow daylight trench in dirt takes 9.3 crew-hours and prices at $1,862.64 -- $46.57 per foot. An 80-foot deep drywell run in clay, with two catch basins, three downspout ties, and a 15-foot driveway crossing, takes 45.3 crew-hours, costs $6,177.40 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator prices it at $8,824.85 -- $110.31 per foot. Quoting the deep job at the shallow job's learned rate of $46.57 per foot gives $3,725.28 for eighty feet, which is $2,452.12 below the deep job's own break-even cost -- before counting the $5,099.58 it falls short of this calculator's price at a 30% target margin.

Is a flat price per foot ever a reasonable shorthand?

For a narrow band of similar jobs -- the same depth, soil, and outlet as the job the rate was learned on -- a per-foot number can land close. The risk is quoting a deeper trench, harder soil, a drywell or storm tie-in, or basins and a driveway crossing the same way sight unseen, because the rate does not know the depth, the soil, or the outlet until the trencher is in the ground, and by then the per-foot number has often already been quoted.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or material costs?

No. It has no data on your local labor market or your supplier's pipe, gravel, or fabric pricing. It takes linear feet, depth, pipe size, soil, the outlet, catch basins, downspout ties, a driveway crossing, and extra solid pipe, plus your own wage, payroll burden, travel, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into crew-hours and a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat per-foot rate skips, not a market survey.

This calculator vs. Jobber

Two different shapes: Jobber is account-based field-service software for running a home-service business across clients, scheduling, and crews. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this French drain cost, given its depth, pipe, soil, and outlet, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

Jobber is field-service management software founded in 2011 and headquartered in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, used by home-service businesses across HVAC, plumbing, electrical, lawn care, and cleaning trades. It combines client management, quoting, scheduling, invoicing, and payment collection into one subscription system meant to run a whole business across every job and every crew, and it says it serves over 200,000 users. It is sold as an ongoing subscription account. Jobber's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — home-service field-service management software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Jobber appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Jobber does. It does not manage clients, schedule crews, send invoices, or collect payments, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes trench depth, pipe size, soil type, daylight versus drywell versus storm tie-in, catch basins, downspout ties, a driveway crossing, and extra solid pipe, plus loaded wage, material rates, and target margin, and turns that into the walk-away price below which the job loses money, a breakdown of where the hours and cost actually go — including how much a deep clay run costs over a shallow dirt trench — and a copyable customer-facing bid summary, plus a printable customer proposal with scope lines and a signature block. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.
